seats.execution: The child multiplies 12 by the top number 2 and never divides by the bottom number 3, giving 24 instead of 8. The fraction is treated as the single number 2. Using it upside down would give 12 × 3 ÷ 2 = 18, not 24.

The child multiplies 24 by the top number 3 and never divides by the bottom number 4, giving 72 instead of 18. The fraction is treated as the single number 3. Using it upside down would give 24 × 4 ÷ 3 = 32, not 72.

The child multiplies 24 by the top number 3 and never divides by the bottom number 4, giving 72 instead of 18. The fraction is treated as the single number 3. Using it upside down would give 24 × 4 ÷ 3 = 32, not 72.

The child uses 40% as 40/100 turned upside down, so works out 60 × 100 ÷ 40 = 150 instead of 60 × 40 ÷ 100 = 24. Multiplying by the bottom number and dividing by the top makes the answer bigger than 60 when 40% of it must be smaller.
The child prices the 3 pencils correctly at 3 × 30p = 90p but never adds the 40p rubber. Taking 90p from £2 gives £1.10 instead of £2 − £1.30 = £0.70.
The child works out the total cost correctly, 3 × 30p + 40p = £1.30, and gives that as the answer. They stop before the last step of taking £1.30 from £2, which gives £0.70 change.
The child takes only the 40p rubber from £2 and never uses the 3 pencils at 30p each. That gives £2 − 40p = £1.60 instead of £2 − £1.30 = £0.70.
The child takes the price of one notebook from £10 and never uses the 3. That gives £10 − £1.45 = £8.55 instead of £10 − £4.35 = £5.65.
The child prices the 4 apples correctly at 4 × 65p = £2.60 but never adds the £2.30 juice. Taking £2.60 from £10 gives £7.40 instead of £10 − £4.90 = £5.10.
The child takes only the £3.60 case from £20 and never uses the £8.75 game. That gives £20 − £3.60 = £16.40 instead of £20 − £12.35 = £7.65.
The child takes only the £1.75 pen from £10 and never uses the £2.65 comic. That gives £10 − £1.75 = £8.25 instead of £10 − £4.40 = £5.60.
The child prices the 7 pencils correctly at 7 × 35p = £2.45 but never adds the £1.80 notebook. Taking £2.45 from £10 gives £7.55 instead of £10 − £4.25 = £5.75.

redrafts.execution: The child takes only the £8.75 game from £20 and never uses the £3.60 case. That gives £20 − £8.75 = £11.25 instead of £20 − £12.35 = £7.65.
The child rounds £8.75 to £9 and £3.60 to £4, then takes £13 from £20. They give the rounded result £7.00 without adjusting back, instead of £7.65.
The child divides 12 by the bottom number 3 and stops there, giving 4 instead of 8. Only one of the two numbers in the fraction is used.
The child turns 2/3 upside down and finds three halves of 12, working out 12 × 3 ÷ 2 = 18. The answer is 12 ÷ 3 × 2 = 8.
The child divides 24 by the bottom number 4 and stops there, giving 6 instead of 18. Only one of the two numbers in the fraction is used.
The child turns 3/4 upside down and finds four thirds of 24, working out 24 × 4 ÷ 3 = 32. The answer is 24 ÷ 4 × 3 = 18.
The child divides 24 by the bottom number 4 and stops there, giving 6 instead of 18. Only one of the two numbers in the fraction is used.

The child writes 40% as 2/5, divides 60 by the bottom number 5 and stops at 12. They never multiply by the top number 2, which gives 24.
The child takes the percentage figure straight off the amount, working out 60 − 40 = 20. The 40 is used as a quantity to subtract rather than as 40 out of every 100, which gives 24.
The child multiplies £1.45 by one fewer notebook, so 2 × £1.45 = £2.90. Taking £2.90 from £10 gives £7.10 instead of £10 − £4.35 = £5.65.
The child works out 3 × £1.45 = £4.35 correctly but adds it to £10 instead of taking it away. That gives £14.35 instead of £5.65 change.
The child rounds 35p up to 40p, so 7 pencils cost £2.80, and adds the £1.80 notebook to make £4.60. They give £10 − £4.60 = £5.40 without adjusting for the 5p added to each pencil, instead of £5.75.
The child multiplies 35p by one fewer pencil, so 6 × 35p = £2.10, then adds the £1.80 notebook to make £3.90. Taking £3.90 from £10 gives £6.10 instead of £5.75.
The child adds 4 × 65p = £2.60 to only the 30p of the £2.30 juice, dropping the £2, to make £2.90. Taking £2.90 from £10 gives £7.10 instead of £10 − £4.90 = £5.10.
The child rounds 65p up to 70p, so 4 apples cost £2.80, and adds the £2.30 juice to make £5.10. They give £10 − £5.10 = £4.90 without adjusting for the 5p added to each apple, instead of £5.10.
The child adds only the 65p of the £2.65 comic to the £1.75 pen, dropping the £2, to make £2.40. Taking £2.40 from £10 gives £7.60 instead of £10 − £4.40 = £5.60.
